Baptism in the Spirit
BAP-tiz-um in thuh SPIR-it
noun phrase
From Latin baptisma (immersion, baptism, from Greek baptisma, a dipping or immersion, from baptizein, to dip, immerse) combined with Old English spīrit (from Latin spiritus, breath, spirit, from spirare, to breathe). The phrase renders the Greek en pneumati baptisthesesthe (you will be baptized in the Spirit, Matt. 3:11; Acts 1:5) and en heni pneumati hemeis pantes eis hen soma ebaptisthemen (in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, 1 Cor. 12:13). Its meaning is disputed between cessationist and continuationist interpretations.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Baptism in the Spirit is the New Testament phrase for the sovereign, effectual work of the Holy Spirit by which the elect are united to Christ and incorporated into His body, the church. Paul states plainly in 1 Corinthians 12:13: “By one Spirit we were all baptized into one body — whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free — and we were all made to drink of one Spirit.” The phrase “all” is decisive: this is not a second, post-conversion experience reserved for a spiritual elite but the foundational, unrepeatable act of the Spirit at conversion by which every believer is joined to Christ and to His body. John the Baptist predicted it: “He who is coming after me” will “baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3:11). Acts 2:4 records the fulfilment of this promise at Pentecost: “They were all filled with the Holy Spirit.”

The Reformed and cessationist understanding is that Spirit baptism is conversion — the initial and unrepeatable indwelling and sealing of the Spirit that marks the transition from death to life. Pentecost was the once-for-all inauguration of the Spirit's new-covenant ministry; individual conversion is each believer's personal participation in what Pentecost inaugurated. The charismatic error is to bifurcate this into two stages — conversion and a subsequent “baptism in the Spirit” evidenced by tongues — making Pentecost an experience to be repeated and the normative Christian life an attenuated first-class citizenship until the second blessing is obtained. First Corinthians 12:13 directly refutes this: all have been baptized in the Spirit, and all drink of one Spirit, without distinction of spiritual status.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defined baptism as “the application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ordinance,” but the baptism in the Spirit is the realities which water baptism signifies: union with Christ, forgiveness, regeneration, and adoption by the Spirit's sovereign act.

expand to see more

BAPTISM, n. [L. baptisma; Gr. baptisma.] The application of water to a person, as a sacrament or religious ordinance, by which he is initiated into the visible church of Christ. The mode and subjects of baptism are matters of controversy among Christians.

In Reformed theology, the outward water of baptism is a sign and seal of the inward reality: regeneration by the Holy Spirit, union with Christ, remission of sins, and adoption into the covenant community.

SPIRIT, n. [L. spiritus.] In theology, the Third Person of the Trinity, the Holy Spirit; the divine agent of regeneration, conviction, sanctification, and the new birth; the One who indwells and seals every believer (Eph. 1:13).

Baptism in the Spirit: the sovereign, inward work by which the Holy Spirit unites the elect sinner to Christ at conversion — the reality that water baptism signifies. This is the event to which John the Baptist pointed: “He will baptize you with the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 3:11).

The Pentecostal and charismatic error: the teaching that Spirit baptism is a second, post-conversion experience evidenced by speaking in tongues, producing a two-tier Christianity of ordinary believers and “spirit-baptized” believers. First Corinthians 12:13 explicitly contradicts this reading.

Key Scripture

1 Cor. 12:13 — "For by one Spirit we were all baptized into one body — whether Jews or Greeks, whether slaves or free — and we were all made to drink of one Spirit."

Matt. 3:11 — "As for me, I baptize you with water for repentance — but He who is coming after me is mightier than I, and I am not fit to remove His sandals. He Himself will baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire."

Acts 2:4 — "And they were all filled with the Holy Spirit, and began to speak with other tongues — as the Spirit was giving them utterance."

Joel 2:28 — "“And it shall come to pass afterward that I will pour out My Spirit on all flesh; your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions."

Modern Corruption

The Pentecostal and charismatic movement has taken a once-for-all conversion reality and recast it as a repeatable post-conversion experience, creating a two-tier Christianity and producing seekers after experiences rather than disciples of Christ.

expand to see more

The Pentecostal doctrine of “baptism in the Holy Spirit” as a second definite work of grace subsequent to conversion, evidenced by speaking in tongues, is the primary corruption of this biblical phrase. The doctrine originated in Charles Parham's Topeka, Kansas, meetings (1901) and was propagated through the Azusa Street Revival (1906) and into classical Pentecostalism (Assemblies of God, Church of God in Christ) and later the Third Wave charismatic movement. It directly contradicts 1 Corinthians 12:13, which makes Spirit baptism the universal experience of all believers at conversion — not a second-tier experience for those who have spoken in tongues. The practical result is a two-class Christianity: “spirit-filled” believers (those with the tongues-experience) and ordinary believers who have not yet “received.” The NT knows no such distinction.

The Neo-Pentecostal and Word of Faith extension of this error adds the claim that full Spirit baptism unleashes supernatural gifts, healings, and prosperity for those who have truly received — turning a doctrine of union with Christ into a technique for spiritual empowerment. The Reformed and cessationist answer is not to deny the Spirit's sovereign work but to recover the biblical definition: Spirit baptism is conversion, Pentecost is inaugurated, and every Christian — including the weakest, the most trembling, the most sin-burdened saint — has been baptized into the body of Christ by one Spirit and drinks of the same Spirit as the most charismatically confident believer in any gathering.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word baptism carries the sense of immersion, submersion, and identification — pointing to the totality of the Spirit's work in joining the believer to Christ at conversion.

expand to see more

Greek baptizein (βαπτίζειν) — to immerse, to dip, to submerge; used of ritual washing, of John's baptism, and of Christ's promise to “baptize” in the Spirit; the basic sense is total immersion, not mere sprinkling

Greek baptisma (βάπτισμα) — the act of immersion; in the New Testament, the standard term for Christian water baptism (the rite) and Spirit baptism (the reality); these are inseparable in meaning but distinguishable in mode

Greek pneuma (πνευμα) — breath, wind, spirit; the standard New Testament word for the Holy Spirit; used both of the Third Person of the Trinity and of the life-giving breath that animates the spiritual body of Christ

Latin spiritus (breath, spirit) — the Latin rendering of pneuma in the Vulgate; entering English as spirit through Old French; the word carries the sense of breath and life as well as personal agency

Latin baptisma — the Vulgate's direct borrowing of the Greek; entering English as baptism through Old French in the 13th century; the theological tradition of both East and West preserved the Greek term rather than translating it, indicating the word's irreplaceable specificity

Usage

"The Westminster Confession (28.1) defines baptism as a sign and seal of regeneration and ingrafting into Christ — the outward ordinance that corresponds to the inward Spirit baptism by which the elect are joined to the covenant Mediator, a connection that secures the Reformed reading of 1 Corinthians 12:13 as conversion rather than post-conversion experience."

"John Owen in A Discourse Concerning the Holy Spirit argued that the Spirit's extraordinary gifts at Pentecost were the inaugural demonstration of the new-covenant Spirit's arrival, not a paradigm to be continually sought or reproduced — the cessationist reading that makes Pentecost a historical hinge rather than a repeatable template."

"The 9Marks movement and Acts 29 network have both addressed the baptism-in-the-Spirit question explicitly in their elder training, insisting that healthy church culture does not pursue a second-blessing experience but calls every believer to walk in the Spirit already received at conversion — a position squarely in the Reformed and cessationist tradition."
